newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro bourses mixed, uncertain over U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro bourses mixed, uncertain over U.S. data.

text.p: European stocks made a mixed showing on Friday with investors wary over U.S. employment figures later in the day which will shed light on inflation pressures.
On currency markets, the dollar climbed half a pfennig on the mark but fell slightly against the yen after remarks by a senior German central banker supporting the Japanese currency.
Most European bourses performed well, apart from London, which dipped on interest rate jitters as data on Britain's economic performance in October registered an 18-month high.

Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Zurich rose strongly after Wall Street posted solid gains on the strength of Thursday's U.S. data suggesting a slowing in the economy, good news for interest rates. Paris was closed because of the All Saints holiday.

London investors took fright when a stronger-than-expected purchasing managers index -- an important guide to economic performance -- raised prospects of more harsh medicine after Wednesday's shock interest rate increase.
"Having seen an interest rate rise this week and comments that we might have another in the future...those numbers took all of the (upward) momentum out of the sytem," said one dealer.

As London's FTSE index slipped 0.3 percent on these figures, investors joined the rest of Europe in switching attention to the U.S. data due at 1330 GMT for clues on the health of the world's biggest economy.
"Most people are betting on a benign number out of the U.S.," said a trader. "If we get it, I think we'll see most markets rally. I don't think we've seen the (stock market's) peaks yet."

The U.S. employment data is watched closely because of its global influence. When June's healthy U.S. payroll data stoked fears of higher interest rates, Wall Street suffered its seventh biggest drop ever, with consequent chaos on European bourses.
"Everyone is just very cautious ahead of these numbers," another added.
In Frankfurt, most investors took an optimistic view. Floor trading was up nearly one percent, encouraged by Wall Street's strong perfromance and stronger bonds market.
But volumes were thin because of a holiday in most areas of Germany and some investors were reluctant to stick their necks out ahead of the U.S. figures.
Amsterdam's EOE index too was up nearly one percent at midday. Swiss stocks also climbed strongly but traders were wary ahead of the U.S. data - "We are all just sitting here waiting," said one.
The dollar strengthened against the mark but was slightly weaker against the yen because of a knock-on effect as the Japanese currency strengthened against the mark.
The mark fell against the yen after Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said a strong yen against the mark would help German exporters.

"The latest pattern is simply to trade off the latest comment you see on the screen -- and the last comment was Welteke's," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Basically he was talking the deutschemark down."

Trading was dampened as currency traders awaited the payrolls figures and the National Association of Purchasing Managers' index at 1500 GMT, the final instalment of the week's heavy schedule of U.S. data.
Although U.S. equity markets have in the past reacted wildly to payrolls data that was out of line with expectations, currency markets have tended to be calmer.
The Swiss franc fell amid talk that Switzerland's banking secrecy laws could be lifted, weakening to 0.8364 per mark from 0.8322 on Thursday and to 1.2723 per dollar from 1.2503.
CURRENCIES AT 1230 GMT
The dollar was trading around 1.5185 marks and 113.62 yen versus 1.5132 and 113.77 in late European business on Thursday.
STOCKS AT 1230 GMT
London's FTSE 100 index was down 13.2 points at 3,965.9.
Germany's DAX index was up 24.00 lower at 2,683.25.
In Paris, markets were closed because of the holiday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $377.35 an ounce, compared to Thursday's close of $379.75. Silver was weaker at $4.80, down six cents.
